## Proof

Let $K$ be a semi-simple quadratic $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra, so $K$ is either a quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ ($d\in\mathbb{Q}^\times$ nonsquare) or the split algebra $\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}$. Let $\rho:K\to M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ be the (left) regular representation and set $T:=\rho(K^\times)\subset GL_2(\mathbb{Q})$. We compute $[N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T):T]$.

**Step 1 — Identify the centralizer.** Since $K$ is a commutative semi-simple $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra of dimension $2$, $\rho(K)\subset M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ is a maximal commutative $\mathbb{Q}$-subalgebra (its dimension $2$ equals half of $\dim_\mathbb{Q} M_2(\mathbb{Q})=4$). Concretely:

- If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with basis $\{1,\sqrt{d}\}$, then $\rho(a+b\sqrt{d})=\begin{pmatrix}a&bd\\ b&a\end{pmatrix}$, and its centralizer in $M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ is $\rho(K)$ itself (the centralizer is a $K$-module inside $M_2(\mathbb{Q})\cong K^2$, and equals $K^{\mathrm{op}}=K$).
- If $K=\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}$, then $\rho(K)$ is the diagonal algebra, whose centralizer in $M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ is again the diagonal algebra $=\rho(K)$.

Hence $C_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(\rho(K))=\rho(K^\times)=T$.

**Step 2 — Reduce the normalizer to algebra automorphisms.** For $g\in N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T)$ we have $gTg^{-1}=T$. Since $T$ spans $\rho(K)$ as a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space (it contains $1$ and elements with arbitrary trace/norm), this is equivalent to $g\rho(K)g^{-1}=\rho(K)$. Conjugation by $g$ then gives a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra automorphism of $\rho(K)\cong K$. Conversely, any $g$ stabilizing the subalgebra $\rho(K)$ normalizes $T$. Thus
$$N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T)=\{g\in GL_2(\mathbb{Q})\;:\;g\rho(K)g^{-1}=\rho(K)\}.$$

**Step 3 — Exact sequence.** The conjugation action yields a homomorphism
$$\varphi:N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K),\qquad g\mapsto\big(x\mapsto \rho^{-1}(g\rho(x)g^{-1})\big).$$
Its kernel is exactly the centralizer $C_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(\rho(K))=T$. So
$$1\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T)\xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;}\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K).$$

**Step 4 — Compute $\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)$ and show surjectivity.** In both cases $\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$:
- field case: $\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})=\{\mathrm{id},\sigma\}$ where $\sigma(\sqrt{d})=-\sqrt{d}$;
- split case: the flip $\tau:(a,b)\mapsto(b,a)$.

These are realized inside $GL_2(\mathbb{Q})$:
- field case: $g=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ satisfies $g\,\rho(a+b\sqrt{d})\,g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&-bd\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}=\rho(\sigma(a+b\sqrt{d}))$;
- split case: $g=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ swaps the two diagonal entries, realizing $\tau$.

So $\varphi$ is surjective, giving
$$N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(T)/T\;\cong\;\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)\;\cong\;\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}.$$

**Conclusion.** In every semi-simple case (field or split) the quotient is cyclic of order $2$, so

$$\boxed{[\,N_{GL_2(\mathbb{Q})}(\rho(K^\times)):\rho(K^\times)\,]=2.}$$

Geometrically this is the Weyl group of the $2$-torus: the normalizer of a maximal torus modulo the torus is the automorphism group of the underlying algebra, which for a quadratic algebra is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
